title: docs: the smoke found a third wall, and it is not code
body:
**#151 worked.** With it deployed, `apt-get update` passes inside the Tide container and the install runs on — to the next wall:

```
curl: (7) Failed to connect to dl.min.io port 443 after 2 ms:
      Could not connect to server
```

Two milliseconds is network-unreachable, not a timeout.

## What is actually true

Checked on the host, `dl.min.io` is the **one** vendor host this platform downloads from that has no AAAA record:

| host | AAAA |
|---|---|
| `deb.debian.org` | `2a04:4e42:400::644` — real |
| `github.com` | `2606:4700:20::ac43:48da` — real |
| `registry-1.docker.io` | `2600:1f18:2148:bc00:…` — real |
| `get.stalw.art` | `2606:4700:3035::ac43:c3b9` — real |
| **`dl.min.io`** | **`::ffff:178.128.69.202` — an IPv4-mapped address, i.e. none** |

All 14 Mesh pools are IPv6-only, so a Tide container cannot reach the only place it fetches MinIO from. **No code change reaches that host.** The options are to mirror the binary somewhere IPv6-reachable (Harbor is right there, and this would be its first real use — see block D), give the pool NAT64/DNS64, or install MinIO from another origin. All three are your call, so this is registered as C3, not attempted.

Also recorded is the trap that made it hard to see: `getent ahostsv6` answers with an IPv4-mapped `::ffff:…` address when there is no AAAA at all. It reads as "this host has IPv6" to anyone skimming. The prefix is the tell.

## Where block A stands

The six modules measure and the three engines without readers refuse with 501 — that part is done and merged. What is still unproven in production is the **measured** path with an engine actually answering, and it is blocked on infrastructure, not on the metrics work: Tide by C3, Flux by C2 (`DATA_PRODUCTS_DEFAULT_NODE` vs `PROXMOX_DEFAULT_NODE`).

Smoke leftovers: none. No container, no DNAT rule, no IP allocation survived; `vmid 104` is gone from the cluster and the records are soft-deleted like any other.

Docs only — no code in this PR.

title: fix(provisioning): one name for the default node
body:
C2 from the block A smoke. Flux provisioned against `"pve"` — a node that does not exist on this cluster — so every attempt died with `Proxmox request timed out` without leaving `requested`. Three clusters went that way during the smoke.

## The cause was not Flux

The setting had **eleven readers in three shapes**:

```ts
PROXMOX_DEFAULT_NODE ?? "pve"                             // 6 modules
DATA_PRODUCTS_DEFAULT_NODE ?? "pve"                       // 2  ← broken
DATA_PRODUCTS_DEFAULT_NODE ?? PROXMOX_DEFAULT_NODE ?? …   // 3
```

Production sets only `PROXMOX_DEFAULT_NODE`, so the second shape fell through to the default. Flux had it — **and so did `getDefaultNode()` in `provisioner-base`**, which means anything reaching for the shared helper inherited the same wrong answer.

Fixing Flux alone would have left nine copies and the same trap for the next module, so the eleven readers become one. `data-products/default-node` accepts either spelling and keeps `"pve"` as the last resort, because that is Proxmox's own default for a single-node install. Every store and the provisioner base re-export it.

## Test

Pins the case that actually broke: `PROXMOX_DEFAULT_NODE` set on its own resolves to that node — exactly how production is configured, and exactly what Flux could not do. Plus the reverse spelling, the precedence when both are set, and the fallback.

`pnpm typecheck` — only the two pre-existing `tests/ignite/{03,04}` errors. Lint — no new findings. `tests/flux/02`, `tests/tide/01` and all of `data-products/`: 110 passing.

## After merge

This unblocks the Flux smoke: a real RabbitMQ cluster, `mc`-equivalent proof from inside, and the **measured** metrics path finally exercised in production — the one part of block A still unproven in the air. Tide stays blocked on C3 (`dl.min.io` has no AAAA); my suggestion for that is in the thread.

title: fix(flux): a broker with no queues has no backlog, and says so
body:
**Block A is proven in the air.** With #153 deployed, the first RabbitMQ cluster to reach `active` in production answered the metrics endpoint with real readings:

```json
"cpuPercent": 0, "memoryPercent": 30, "diskPercent": 8,
"messagesPerSec": 0, "queueCount": 0, "connectionCount": 0,
"messagesReady": null, "messagesUnacked": null,
"unavailable": []
```

Container measured by Proxmox, broker measured through the management API, `unavailable` empty because everything was actually read. The zeros are measured zeros — a fresh broker with no queues, no connections, nothing published between the two samples.

## And the smoke caught a defect in my own parser

`messagesReady` and `messagesUnacked` came back **null with an empty `unavailable`**. On screen that is two "—" tiles with nothing beside them explaining why: the exact "a grid of dashes reads as *nothing is happening* rather than *nobody could read this*" failure this module was written to prevent, reintroduced by its own parser.

RabbitMQ omits `queue_totals` entirely on a broker with no queues — the same way it omits `message_stats` before anything is published. The `message_stats` case was already read as zero and documented; this one was read as unknown. A broker with no queues has nothing waiting in them, and that is a reading, not a gap. When queues **do** exist and the totals are missing, it stays null, because then it really is a gap.

Plus a net under all of it: if any field comes back unmeasured and nothing in `unavailable` accounts for it, the response now says so rather than leaving the screen to imply zero.

No test would have caught this. The suites only ever see an unreachable broker, where every field is null for one obvious reason that *is* named. It took a real cluster answering. Both shapes are now covered by parser tests.

## Smoke record

Provisioned through the client path, measured, destroyed, verified: no container, no DNAT rule, no leftovers. The two refusal records (redpanda, nats) are soft-deleted like the rest.

`pnpm typecheck` — only the two pre-existing `tests/ignite/{03,04}` errors. `tests/flux/02` plus the parser suite: 57 passing.

title: fix(nexus): stop blaming a restart that never happened
body:
The first ScyllaDB cluster to reach `active` in production answered:

```json
"cpuPercent": 3, "memoryPercent": 66, "diskPercent": 11,
"nodeState": "UN", "nodeHealthy": true,
"readOpsPerSec": null, "writeOpsPerSec": null,
"unavailable": ["Operation rates: the two samples of ScyllaDB's counters could not
  be compared, which happens when the node restarted between them."]
```

The good half: the container was measured by Proxmox and **`nodetool status` parsed correctly against real output** — `UN`, healthy. That is the ring parser proven in the air.

The bad half: **the explanation is false.** Nothing restarted. A brand-new cluster simply has no keyspace of its own yet — and there was already a branch saying exactly that, which could never run.

## Why the honest branch was unreachable

`keyspaces` used `null` for "tablestats did not answer" and an empty array for "no user keyspaces", but `readScyllaMetrics` collapsed both into `null`:

```ts
keyspaces: after.length > 0 ? after : before.length > 0 ? before : null
```

So the `keyspaces.length === 0` branch never fired and control fell through to the restart message. Those are different facts and they now travel separately: `tablestatsRead` says whether the command produced anything at all, `keyspaces` is the filtered list. ScyllaDB always has internal keyspaces, so any `Keyspace :` block is proof the command ran, even when every one of them is filtered out for being ScyllaDB's own.

## Why this is the same defect one level up

A wrong explanation is worse than a vague one: it sends an operator looking for a restart that never happened, and it looks authoritative doing it. This module exists to stop invented numbers; an invented *reason* is the same failure wearing different clothes.

No test would have caught it — the suites only ever see an unreachable node, where that branch is never reached. It took a real cluster answering. `sawAnyKeyspace` is now covered directly, including the case that matters (ScyllaDB's own keyspaces as proof of life) and the prose false-positive.

## Smoke record

ScyllaDB provisioned through the client path → measured → destroyed. FerretDB created afterwards, sequentially (`/cluster/nextid` does not reserve — C4), refused with **501** and the SQLite-handler explanation, then destroyed. No container, no DNAT rule, no leftovers: `vmid 104` gone, no `8104` rule.

`pnpm typecheck` — only the two pre-existing `tests/ignite/{03,04}` errors. `tests/nexus/02` plus the parser suite: 53 passing.

title: docs: deleting a resource does not give the quota back
body:
Two findings from today's smoke. Both registered, neither fixed — they need a decision, not a patch.

## C5 — deleted resources hold quota forever 🔴

Re-provisioning in the same org was refused:

```
TIER_LIMIT_EXCEEDED — "Cluster limit reached for tier starter (max: 2)"
  details: { tier: "starter", current: 2 }
```

**Both clusters it counted were `deleted`.** Nexus, Atlas, Spark and Tide all call `store.listClusters({ orgId })` / `listInstances({ orgId })` with no status filter and pass `.length` straight to `checkTierLimit`. The soft delete keeps the row, so the row keeps counting.

For a customer on the starter tier (max 2): create two resources, delete both, and you can never create another. **Deleting frees nothing**, and the screen just refuses without explaining why. Every module that enforces a tier limit has it.

The obvious fix is to stop counting `deleted` — but the question underneath is whether a resource in `deleting` or `failed` should hold quota, and that one has a less obvious answer. Hence a decision rather than a patch.

Found by trying to re-provision in the same org during the smoke; worked around with a fresh `orgId`.

## C6 — three Settings links lead to 404

| module | menu entry | page exists |
|---|---|---|
| Spark | yes | yes |
| Atlas | yes | yes |
| **Nexus** | yes | **no** |
| **Tide** | yes | **no** |
| **Flux** | yes | **no** |

The manifests declare `/{module}/settings`; there is no `page.tsx` for any of the three. The signature defect of this codebase again — the screen promising what does not exist.

Either remove the three entries (honest, small) or build the pages with Atlas and Spark as the mould, which is product work and needs to know what each one should actually adjust.

Docs only — no code in this PR.

title: feat(tide): a way out for a container that only has IPv6
body:
C3, option (a). Every Mesh pool here is IPv6-only — which is why a Tide container needs no DNAT to be reached, and why it cannot reach `dl.min.io`, which has no AAAA record. MinIO could never be downloaded, so no Tide instance ever finished provisioning:

```
curl: (7) Failed to connect to dl.min.io port 443 after 2 ms
```

Two milliseconds is network-unreachable wearing a connection error's clothes.

## What changes

The container keeps its public IPv6 on `eth0` for inbound and gains a private IPv4 on `eth1` purely to get out.

**This costs no public address.** `172.10.0.0/24` is RFC1918 and the host has masqueraded it out of its single public IPv4 since this cluster existed:

```
-A POSTROUTING -s 172.10.0.0/24 -o vmbr0 -j MASQUERADE
```

That is how every other guest installs packages. Two default routes, one per address family; they do not compete.

## Two details that would have bitten

**`firewall=0` is not decoration.** With `firewall=1` Proxmox builds an `fwbr` bridge in front of the NIC and NAT egress breaks inside an unprivileged LXC — apt then fails with "Could not resolve host", the exact symptom this interface exists to remove. `eth0` pins it for the same documented reason; a test pins it here so it cannot quietly come back.

**The address is allocated, never guessed.** `allocateLxcIp` scans every guest's every NIC and throws rather than fall back to a scheme that cannot see what is taken. That matters more than usual here: `vmbr1` is one L2 spanning both nodes, so a duplicate address is not a clash, it is a black hole for whoever loses the ARP race.

## Scope

Tide only. Spark installs over apt and Email uses a host with IPv6 — both work today, and touching them would be risk without a defect. The helper lives in `data-products/egress.ts` so the next module that hits this wall inherits it rather than reinventing it.

## On NAT64

Still the larger, better answer: it fixes this for every IPv6-only guest at once and needs no second NIC. It also cannot help anything dialling a literal IPv4 address, since nothing asks DNS then, and DNS64 costs you DNSSEC validation on synthesized records. This is the smaller, reversible move — it comes out by deleting one line the day NAT64 lands.

## After merge

Deploy, then the Tide smoke that has never been possible: a real MinIO answering `mc admin info`, which is the last unproven piece of block A. Worth flagging that Tide's two parsers have never seen real output, and the equivalent parsers in Flux and Nexus **both** had defects that only a live engine exposed.

`pnpm typecheck` — only the two pre-existing `tests/ignite/{03,04}` errors. Lint — no new findings.

title: fix(data-products): pct exec has no /usr/local/bin, and it shows
body:
**#157 worked.** The first Tide instance ever to reach `active` came up exactly right — `eth1 172.10.0.219/24` beside the public IPv6, MinIO and `mc` in `/usr/local/bin`, the server listening on `:9000`, and a bucket holding two objects I uploaded to it.

And every command the product runs inside that container could not find `mc`:

```
$ pct exec 104 -- bash -c 'echo PATH=$PATH; command -v mc || echo NOT-FOUND'
PATH=/sbin:/bin:/usr/sbin:/usr/bin
NOT-FOUND
```

`/usr/local/bin` is not on it — which is precisely where this platform installs the binaries it later depends on.

## Why this is a lie, not an error

The metrics reader opens with `command -v mc >/dev/null 2>&1 || exit 127`. So it exits, `result.ok` is false, and the response says MinIO **"did not answer `mc admin info`"** — about a container where `mc` is sitting in `/usr/local/bin`, executable, next to a running server. The operator goes and looks at a healthy service.

The Tide credential path has the same shape (`which mc || curl…` then a bare `mc alias set`) and would have failed the same way. It predates this work; no Tide instance had ever existed to hit it.

## Fixed at the seam

`execInContainer` now prepends the PATH, so every provisioner inherits it, and the metrics reader — which goes through `remote-exec` directly — prepends the same exported constant. Adding a directory takes none away, so nothing that works today changes: `rabbitmqctl` in `/usr/sbin` and `docker` in `/usr/bin` are untouched.

## Also documented: `admin info` lags

Right after uploading, `admin info` reported `buckets: 0, objects: 0, usage: 0`. Minutes later, `buckets: 1, objects: 2, usage: 8000000` — the real figures. Those counts come from MinIO's background scanner. That is a lag in what MinIO knows rather than a gap in what we read, so it stays a number and is now documented as such instead of quietly surprising the next reader.

## Verification plan

The container from the smoke is **still up** on purpose. After merge and deploy I will read metrics against it — a live MinIO with a bucket, two objects and a request counter that already shows traffic — which is the last unproven piece of block A. Then destroy it and confirm nothing is left.

No test could have found this. It needed a container with software installed where this platform installs software. `tests/tide/03` (37) and the parser suites pass; typecheck shows only the two pre-existing `tests/ignite/{03,04}` errors.

title: fix(nav): three Settings links that led nowhere
body:
C6. Nexus, Tide and Flux each declare a Settings entry in their module manifest — gear icon and all — and none of them has a page. Clicking any of the three gives a 404. Spark, Atlas, Mesh, Pulse and Aegis have real pages; these three never did.

## Why remove rather than build

**There is nothing to configure.** Every knob these modules have lives in an environment variable read at boot — `DATA_PRODUCTS_STORAGE`, the default node, the store backend — none of it editable at runtime. A Settings page here would have to invent controls that adjust nothing, which is the defect this codebase keeps producing, not a fix for it.

## One thing worth deciding separately

While checking what the "mould" looked like: **Atlas's and Spark's Settings pages are not settings either.** They are static roadmaps — a hardcoded list of waves marked shipped/planned — sitting behind a gear icon that promises configuration. Same family of defect, milder version. Renaming those two entries to "Roadmap" would make the label true, and it is two lines.

Left alone in this PR because it changes two screens that currently work, and that is your call, not mine.

## If you do want real Settings somewhere

Tell me what should be adjustable and I will build it against a real source — a value that is read back from where it actually lives, not a form that writes to nothing.

`pnpm typecheck` — only the two pre-existing `tests/ignite/{03,04}` errors. No test referenced the removed entries.

title: fix(core): the encrypted store stopped writing above ~64 KB
body:
The 🔴 finding that has been sitting in the kickoff. `encrypt()` ended with:

```ts
btoa(String.fromCharCode(...result))
```

Spreading a large `Uint8Array` blows V8's argument limit. **Measured on this Node 22: the spread succeeds at 65536 bytes and throws at 131072** with `RangeError: Maximum call stack size exceeded`.

## Why the symptom is worse than a crash

`decrypt()` never spread anything. So a store file that grew past the ceiling still **read** fine while every **write** failed — the data on disk silently froze at its last small version and new events were logged as lost. That is exactly what the dev `.herald-events-store.json` does on every test round: `[Herald] FAILED to persist event … this event is lost`.

Production runs `STORE_BACKEND=postgres` and does not hit it. The code default is `json`, so any deployment that leaves the default is one large store away from the same silent freeze.

## The fix, and why it is compatible

Chunked `String.fromCharCode` over the **binary string**, with `btoa` still called exactly **once** over the whole assembled string. That is what makes compatibility structural rather than a promise: the encoder is the same pure function it always was for every input the old code could handle. No per-chunk base64 (which would have needed 3-byte-aligned chunks to be safe), and AES-GCM parameters, PBKDF2 salt and iterations, and the IV-prepended framing are untouched.

I verified the byte-identity independently of the test suite — old spread vs new chunked encoder across 0, 1, 2, 3, 17, 255, 32767, 32768, 32769, 65535 and 65536 bytes, covering both chunk seams and all three padding remainders: identical everywhere.

So every `.{module}-store.json` and `.connections.json` on disk keeps decrypting, and — asserted in both directions in the suite — a store written by this build stays readable by a process still running the old one, which makes a rollback or a stale worker safe.

`Buffer` was the other option and was deliberately not used: `packages/core` is ESM-only plain `tsc` with `DOM` libs and is reachable from browser/edge bundles, where `Buffer` does not exist. `btoa`/`atob` were already the only globals this file assumed beyond `crypto`.

## Tests

`packages/core` had no test runner; there is one now (vitest, matching the root's existing `test:db-migrate` / `test:ship` pattern), with 15 tests: round-trips at 1 MB and across the chunk seams, a frozen golden ciphertext from the pre-fix code, old→new and new→old decryption, direct encoder equality across 17 sizes, and the two rejection paths.

**The suite was confirmed to pin the defect**: restoring the spread makes exactly the 1 MB and 131072-byte cases fail and the other 13 still pass — which is precisely how a small-payloads-only suite let this ship in the first place.

`scripts/migrate-stores/state/crypto.ts` carries a deliberate byte-for-byte copy of this module and reads the real (large) store files, so it got the same fix; its 206 migration tests pass.

`apps/web` typecheck shows only the two pre-existing `tests/ignite/{03,04}` errors. The `pnpm-lock.yaml` diff includes a few lines of unrelated registry metadata churn (deprecation strings) alongside the vitest entry.

title: fix(provisioning): two creates in the same second no longer collide
body:
C4, seen live in today's smoke: three Flux clusters created in the same second, all three handed vmid 104, one survived and two died permanently.

```
Failed to create LXC: 500 {"message":"CT 104 already exists on node 'sp1-sd-catalisatec-2'"}
```

`getNextVmid()` is a bare GET of `/cluster/nextid`. That endpoint reports the lowest free id and **does not reserve it**, so concurrent provisions read the same number, the loser gets the 500, and the resource is marked `failed` with no second attempt. This is what happens to anyone clicking create three times, or to any batch provisioning.

## The fix

`createLxcWithFreshVmid(node, buildConfig, options)` reads an id, creates, and on that specific conflict discards the id and re-reads `/cluster/nextid`. Bounded at 5 attempts with a jittered pause, so two losers of the same race do not re-read in lockstep.

Two details that make it correct rather than merely hopeful:

**`buildConfig` is a function of the candidate vmid, called per attempt.** Flux and Nexus derive their IP from `allocateLxcIp(node, vmid)` and Tide derives its egress NIC from `ipv4EgressNic({ node, vmid })`. A config built once against the losing id would have put that id's address on the winning container — a duplicate IP on vmbr1, which is one L2 spanning both nodes, is not a clash but a black hole for whoever loses the ARP race.

**Only the collision is retried.** Anything else rethrows on the first attempt, and a test asserts exactly one create call for a non-collision error — retrying a real failure would turn one clear error into five confusing ones.

A side effect worth having: the predicate also matches `volume '…' already exists`, which is what a stale-dm orphan disk produces. There are 11 of those on this cluster; a fresh vmid dodges them instead of failing.

Adopted in the three provisioners the smoke exercises — Tide, Flux, Nexus. Their persistence of `lxcIds` and their rollback paths work on the id that actually took.

## Deliberately not fixed, and worth knowing

**Nine other call sites have the identical defect** — Atlas (two: primary and replica, so a multi-node Atlas can collide *with itself*), Beacon (two, plus its orchestrator), Blaze, Email, Herald, Ignite, Launch, Spark, and two in the Mesh runtime adapter. Adoption is mechanical for most; Atlas's replica loop deserves thought because a mid-loop retry interacts with its own rollback. Not touched here because they cannot be exercised the way Tide/Flux/Nexus just were.

**The retry narrows the window, it does not close it.** Two provisions can still both read the new id after the winner lands. Five attempts converge for small batches; a large simultaneous batch could still exhaust them. The durable fix is a reserving allocator — the same shape as `mesh/ipam-engine`, which already exists for IP addresses.

**Unrelated, found in passing (registering, not fixing):** Flux and Nexus call `addPortForward(...)` without awaiting it (`flux/provisioner.ts:183,189`, `nexus/provisioner.ts:141`). That function was made awaitable and result-returning on 2026-08-15 precisely so failures stop being invisible; these two call sites never got updated, so a failed port-forward there is still silently dropped. Tide awaits it correctly. This is the same family as the open "publish does not check its result before marking active" finding.

10 new tests pass; `data-products/` suite green; typecheck shows only the two pre-existing `tests/ignite/{03,04}` errors; lint clean on every touched file.

title: fix(mesh): a conditional hook on the services page
body:
Item 5 of the closed list said "13 rules-of-hooks errors". The count was right and the reading was wrong: **twelve of them were not React at all**, and the thirteenth was a real crash.

## The real bug — one component

`src/app/(dashboard)/mesh/services/page.tsx`. `PageContent` returned `null` early to let the `?create=` redirect take over, and then called `useMemo` twice below that return. Any visit carrying `?create=load_balancer|ingress|api_gateway` rendered with two fewer hooks than the visit before it — the exact shape that throws and hands the user "Something went wrong", which is how the Herald tab fell over.

Both `useMemo` calls moved above the bail-out and the `return null` moved below them, with a comment saying why the order matters. The repeated inline condition became one `isCreateRedirect` const so the effect and the return cannot drift apart. Rendered output is unchanged.

## The twelve that were not React

`usePostgres()` — a module-private predicate in `src/lib/server/deploy/current-store.ts`, `deploy/store.ts` and `sshkeys/store.ts`. Pure server code, no component in sight, but the `use` prefix made the linter treat every call as a hook call. Renamed to `isPostgresBacked()`, which also matches the `StoreBackend` vocabulary next door in `src/lib/server/db/`. Not exported anywhere, so the rename is entirely local: same env lookup, same boolean.

Worth correcting in the kickoff — "13 conditional hooks" sounds like thirteen tabs waiting to die, and it was one.

## What is left, deliberately

15 `rules-of-hooks` errors remain, **all in `tests/`**, every one the `useTestSession` helper called at module top level: the same naming false positive, in files that never render. Verified after the fix: zero left in `src/`.

**`set-state-in-effect` is untouched, as scoped** — 36 errors across 35 files. They share one shape: a dialog seeding form state from props in an effect. The SDN dialogs and the `src/components/` dialogs are the dense clusters. Because it is one repeated pattern, the `useSyncExternalStore` conversion is a single change applied 35 times rather than 35 separate problems.

`build` succeeds (149/149 static pages, `/mesh/services` among them); typecheck shows only the two pre-existing `tests/ignite/{03,04}` errors.

**Environment note worth keeping:** in a git worktree, the root `corepack pnpm typecheck` fails with "Unable to find package manager binary" before running anything — turbo shells out to a real `pnpm` on PATH, which corepack does not provide. That failure is not a code failure.

title: fix(data-products): deleting a resource gives the quota back
body:
C5 — the finding with a customer on the other end. Production refused a create with:

```
TIER_LIMIT_EXCEEDED — "Cluster limit reached for tier starter (max: 2)"
  details: { current: 2 }      ← both of them status "deleted"
```

Deletes here are soft, and four modules — Nexus, Atlas, Spark, Tide — counted quota by listing on `orgId` alone and handing `.length` to `checkTierLimit`, so the tombstones counted. **A starter org that created two resources and deleted both was permanently at its limit**, with no transition out of `deleted` and so nothing the tenant could do to free it.

## `deleted` is the only status that releases

That asymmetry is deliberate and documented in the new `data-products/quota.ts`:

- **`failed` still counts** — provisioning died partway and the LXC it already created is very often still on the node. Freeing the slot there lets a tenant loop create → fail → create and accumulate real containers well past what they pay for.
- **`deleting` still counts** — the teardown is in flight and the container exists right now. Releasing early lets the replacement be provisioned alongside it.

One helper rather than four copies of a filter, for the reason this repo keeps relearning — the same logic in N places diverges in N ways (see `dns.ts`, `default-node.ts`, and the eleven copies of the default-node reader fixed yesterday). Nexus and Atlas also had a misleading `details.current` in the error payload; that now reports the number actually used.

## A worse variant, found and NOT fixed

**Ignite and Blaze have the same defect in a form that cannot be fixed the same way.** Both count an unfiltered org listing, but their status unions have no terminal `deleted` state at all — and a *successful* deprovision writes the record back as **`failed`** (`ignite/provisioner.ts:154`, `blaze/provisioner.ts:174`).

So in those two modules a cleanly deleted function is indistinguishable from a broken one, and holds its quota slot forever. Dropping this helper in would not help: they need a terminal status added and the deprovisioner corrected first.

The connection worth noticing: the long-standing pre-existing typecheck error in `tests/ignite/04-lifecycle.integration.test.ts` is a test reaching for a `"deleted"` status that does not exist. That error has been sitting in the baseline as noise; it is this gap surfacing.

## Tests

11 unit tests on the helper, plus a matching pair in each of the four service suites: one proving create → delete → create no longer exhausts quota, one proving `failed` and `deleting` still block at the cap. No existing test was pinning the old behaviour — the existing "2 existing clusters → TIER_LIMIT_EXCEEDED" cases all use `requested` records, which still count.

Suites run: 99 + 140 + 149 passing across the unit, service and route layers. Typecheck shows only the two pre-existing `tests/ignite/{03,04}` errors. Lint clean on the new files.

title: fix(herald): the export refuses instead of pretending
body:
Item 5's "Herald export is fake". `createExportJob` saved a job, then a `setTimeout` flipped it to `running` and, 2.5 seconds later, to `completed` with `downloadUrl: /api/herald/export/{id}/download` — **a route that does not exist anywhere in this repo.** No GET handler, no writer, no file. The Events screen had an Export button, a success toast, and a polling hook that watched the timer report success. Every format produced the same dead link.

## Refusing, the way this codebase already refuses

New `lib/data-products/herald-export-support.ts`, the sibling of `metrics-support.ts` and `credential-support.ts`: one client-safe fact that the endpoint and the screen both read. `POST /api/herald/export` answers **501 NOT_IMPLEMENTED** with a message naming the working alternative — `GET /api/herald/events` takes the same filters and returns JSON, and the `herald_events` table is there on the Postgres backend.

The refusal applies to any body. Validating the format of an export that will never run only tells the caller their impossible request was well-formed.

**The screen loses the button**, replaced by the reason. An honest 501 behind an inviting button is still a screen telling the user something untrue.

## The dormant state is gone, not left lying around

`HeraldExportJob` and its enums, the `exportJobs` store collection and its accessors, the create schema, the Postgres adapter branches, the drizzle table, and the migrate-stores mapper. Keeping them would leave the next reader believing exports exist.

## ⚠️ This includes a destructive migration — your call

`0035_drop_herald_export_jobs.sql` drops `herald_meta_export_jobs` and its two enums. It is idempotent, drops the table before the types (Postgres refuses otherwise), and nothing references it — the FK points the other way, to `herald_meta_instances`.

**Every row in that table records a completion that did not happen**, which is worse than no row: kept around it reads as export history. But it is a DROP, so review the SQL line by line as the runbook says, and note that merging this does not apply it — the operator runs `db:apply` when they choose. The code works either way; the table simply has no writer left.

## Tests

The suites that pinned the fake success were rewritten, each with a comment saying that is what they were doing: `tests/herald/02` (refuses, no payload, names the alternative, not retryable), `tests/herald/03` (501 for every format, invalid format also 501 rather than 400, nothing persisted, `GET /export/:jobId` is route-not-found), `tests/herald/01` (the export-job CRUD suite retired; the store-shape test now asserts `exportJobs` is absent).

One assertion needed care: `expect(serialised).not.toContain("downloadUrl")` failed against the refusal *message*, which names the dead URL on purpose. The checks now inspect the payload rather than the prose, with a comment explaining why.

87 passing / 11 skipped in `tests/herald/` (05-e2e needs a live server), 202 in migrate-stores, 106 across herald + db + data-products. Typecheck: only the two pre-existing `tests/ignite/{03,04}` errors. Lint clean on touched files.

**Found, not fixed:** `components/herald/instance-create-dialog.tsx:79` calls `Date.now()` during render for a requestId — pre-existing lint error, unrelated to export. And `.herald-store.json` files on disk still carry a legacy `exportJobs` key; the JSON backend ignores it and nothing reads it.

title: docs: the wave of six, and the three findings it surfaced
body:
Records the six PRs that shipped today (#159–#164) and — more usefully — what running five agents over this code turned up.

## Two entries in the kickoff were wrong

**"13 rules-of-hooks errors"** read like thirteen tabs waiting to die. Twelve were a server-side predicate named `usePostgres()` that the linter treated as a hook because of the prefix; the real bug was **one** component. Corrected, because that difference changes how you'd budget the work.

**`set-state-in-effect`** is 36 errors across 35 files, not a footnote — but they share a single shape (a dialog seeding form state from props in an effect), so it is one repeated pattern applied 35 times, not 35 problems.

## Three new findings, registered not fixed

**C7 🔴 — Ignite and Blaze write a *successful* deprovision back as `failed`**, and neither has a terminal status at all. So a cleanly deleted function is indistinguishable from a broken one on screen, and holds its quota slot forever. The quota helper from #163 cannot be dropped in until a terminal status exists.

The part worth noticing: the typecheck error in `tests/ignite/04` that has sat in the baseline as noise is a test reaching for the `"deleted"` status that does not exist. It was never dirt — it was this defect surfacing, and it has been visible in every typecheck run for weeks.

**C8 — nine provisioners still carry the vmid race**, Atlas twice, where a multi-node cluster can collide with itself. And the retry narrows the window rather than closing it; the durable fix is a reserving allocator, the shape `mesh/ipam-engine` already has for IPs.

**C9 — Flux and Nexus never got updated when `addPortForward` became awaitable** (2026-08-15), so a failed port-forward there is still silently dropped. Tide awaits it correctly.

## Both provable fixes were proven in production

- **#161** — three Flux clusters created **20 ms apart** all reached `active`, on distinct vmids 104, 107 and 106. The allocator skipped 105, which is the live `traefik-gateway`. This morning the identical scenario gave one active and two dead with `CT 104 already exists`.
- **#163** — the Nexus `org-smoke`, holding two `deleted` clusters that blocked it, accepted the same request that returned `TIER_LIMIT_EXCEEDED` this morning.

Everything created for those smokes is destroyed and verified: no containers on vmid 104/106/107, no DNAT rules in the Flux range.

The other four (#159, #160, #162, #164) have no smoke — they are a screen, a library, a refusal and a nav change, verified by test and build.

Docs only.

title: fix(provisioning): the vmid retry, everywhere else
body:
C8. #161 fixed the vmid race in Tide, Flux and Nexus. This adopts `createLxcWithFreshVmid` in the ten sites that remained: Atlas (2), Beacon (2 + its orchestrator), Email, Herald, Launch, Spark, and the Mesh runtime adapter (2).

After this, `getNextVmid` appears only in `provisioner-base.ts` and its own tests — except Ignite and Blaze, deliberately left because another change is editing those two files.

## Two sites that needed more than a rewrite

**Atlas's replica loop — adopted, with an argument.** I asked for it to be left if it could not be shown safe. It can: there is no per-iteration rollback, the outer `catch` calls `releaseClusterAllocations(clusterId)` which matches on `serviceId` and knows nothing about vmids, and nothing about a replica is persisted until its container exists. The real interaction was ordering — `getNextVmid()` used to run *before* `reserveAddress()`, so a naive adoption would burn one Mesh address per failed attempt. The reservation is hoisted above the create instead.

**Launch needed a reorder.** It wrote the replica row — which carries `vmid` — *before* the create. Both `rollbackReplica` and `deprovisionReplica` stop and delete by that field, so a persisted losing id would have torn down whichever container **won** the race. The row is now written after the create, against the id that took.

The general rule applied per site: where the address is derived from the id (`allocateLxcIp` — Beacon ×2, Herald), it is derived **inside** the per-attempt callback; where it comes from a Mesh reservation (Atlas, Email, Launch, Spark), the reservation stays **outside** so a retry reuses it instead of leaking a second one.

## Test

Rather than re-testing the helper (already covered), the new test drives **Herald's real provisioner with the real helper**, faking only Proxmox through the helper's existing `deps` seam — mocking the helper itself would assert nothing. Herald is the subject because both its address and its published port are vmid-derived, so a config built against the losing id is visible: the test pins that the losing attempt carried `172.10.0.104/24`, the winning one `172.10.0.105/24`, `lxcIds === [105]`, and the endpoint landed on `:4105`.

`tests/mesh/09` needed updating — it replaced `provisioner-base` wholesale with a strict mock; it now delegates to the real helper through `deps`, preserving its vmid sequence.

## Found, not fixed

Atlas has an orphan bug unrelated to vmids: the local `lxcIds` array is only persisted at step 8, so a replica that fails mid-loop leaves the store holding `[primaryVmid]` while already-created replica containers are orphaned — the failure path releases IPs but never deletes those containers.

208 tests pass in the stated command; 369 more across every touched module; typecheck shows only the pre-existing ignite errors; lint clean on touched files.

title: fix(provisioning): a published endpoint that was never checked
body:
The 🔴 "publish does not check its result before marking active", in its two concrete cases: Flux (two forwards) and Nexus fired `addPortForward` without awaiting it. The function was made awaitable and result-returning on 2026-08-15 precisely so this would stop being invisible; these call sites never got updated. The cluster went `active` and advertised an address that may forward nothing, with nothing anywhere saying why. On this host the failure is real — the publish has lost the race for `/run/xtables.lock` against Docker before, which is why the iptables calls carry `-w 5`.

## The failure behaviour, and why

On a failed publish: status `degraded`, **the endpoint is not stored**, and the Herald event drops to `partial` with prose naming the port, the underlying error, and the intended address.

- **Not `failed`** — the container is up and the engine installed; only a host NAT rule is missing. Decisively, `degraded` is in `LIVE_STATUSES` in `network/desired-state.ts`, so the reconciler keeps re-applying the rule and the cluster is repairable in place. `failed` would strand it outside reconciliation.
- **Endpoint withheld rather than stored** — the UI renders the connection panel on `cluster.endpoint` alone, with no reference to status. A stored endpoint *is* a published one to the user, so keeping it while degraded would still hand over a copyable string that refuses connections. The intended address goes in the event, where it informs without inviting.
- **Flux's two forwards are independent** — if only the management UI fails, the broker endpoint is kept and the management port withheld. Withholding a working broker address would be its own lie.

## ⚠️ A correction to #161's description, and to mine

**Tide does NOT await `addPortForward`.** I wrote in #161 that it did and used it as the reference in briefing this work; that was wrong — `tide/provisioner.ts:263` fires it unawaited and publishes the endpoint on the next line. Atlas was used as the shape reference instead.

So the same defect remains at: `tide:263`, `spark:567`, `herald:149`, `email:289` (in a loop over every mail port, so any of ~5 forwards can vanish), and `ignite:84` (excluded — another change owns that file). A follow-up covers them.

**And `atlas:574` is a half-fix**: it awaits and inspects the result, then only `console.error`s and marks the cluster `active` with its endpoint anyway. A log line nobody reads is not an operator-visible signal, so the original finding still stands for Atlas.

**Related, worth its own fix:** `desired-state.ts:126` declares Nexus's internal port as 8081, while the provisioner uses 9042 (ScyllaDB) or 27017 (FerretDB). Nothing listens on 8081, so the reconciler's repair for Nexus currently installs a rule into a black hole — which weakens the repair path this change leans on for that one module.

## Test

7 new tests. Verified as a real guard by stashing the fix and re-running: **5 of 7 fail on the old code**, and the two happy-path controls still pass, so it also pins that healthy clusters are not over-degraded.

164 tests pass across the required suites; typecheck shows only the pre-existing ignite errors; zero lint findings in the three touched files.

title: fix(atlas): a credential nobody recorded, for a door nobody said was locked
body:
Two findings that turn out to be the same problem seen from either end: issuing a database identity left no trace, and the identity it issued could not connect without a firewall rule the screen never mentioned.

## The audit

Atlas emitted 11 kinds of Herald event and **not one about a credential** — it was the only data product issuing database identities into silence. Creation and revocation now write to **both** trails: Herald (`credential.created` / `credential.revoked`, matching what Flux, Nexus, Spark and Tide already emit) and the Aegis audit store (`atlas.credential.created` / `.revoked`), which is the trail you actually query after an incident to ask who was granted access to what.

The actor is the **session**, not `cluster.createdBy` — the route now passes `session.actorId` through. The audit write is awaited before the caller is handed a password, so the record exists before the secret does.

The event carries cluster, org, username, database and the access verdict below. It never carries the password, the hash, or a prefix of either — and a test asserts the serialized event contains none of them.

## The screen

Atlas rebuilds `pg_hba` from `atlas_firewall_rules`, so a credential with no rule admitting its origin means the user exists and cannot connect. That separation is deliberate by design; the silence about it was not. The user got working credentials that failed at first use with `no pg_hba.conf entry for host` — an error pointing nowhere near the cause.

The new notice reports the **current** state, read from the existing firewall-rules endpoint, in one of three shapes: no rules at all, rules scoped only to other roles, or rules in the wrong address family. That last one is the live case on CT 147 — an IPv4 `/32` on an IPv6-only endpoint, a rule that is present and inert.

**It renders nothing when a rule could admit**, which matters: a false accusation sends people to delete rules that work. It appears on the Credentials tab, on the Connect tab (which hands out a DSN), and in the create dialog beside the password, where the username is known so role scoping counts. Discovered clusters show nothing — Atlas neither wrote nor can read their pg_hba.

The verdict lives in a client-safe module called by both the service and the screen, so the audit trail and the UI cannot drift into telling different stories.

## Found along the way

**`.audit-store.json` had no path override**, so running the Atlas suite appended real test events to the developer's actual audit file. Fixed with `AUDIT_STORE_PATH`, mirroring every other store — the only file touched outside Atlas, and worth knowing your local audit store may already have test rows in it.

Not fixed, all real: `regeneratePgHba` writes `deny` rules as `hostnossl`, which is not a deny — an SSL-less client still authenticates. And `revokeAtlasCredential` never `DROP`s or `NOLOGIN`s the Postgres user, so revocation is a store-only tombstone and **a revoked credential keeps working against the database**. That one deserves its own entry.

213 tests pass; typecheck shows only the pre-existing ignite errors; build clean; zero new lint findings.

title: fix(ignite,blaze): a successful delete stops being recorded as a failure
body:
C7, the worst thing still open. `deprovisionFunction` and `deprovisionWorker` wrote the record back as **`failed`** when the teardown had *succeeded* — because neither product had a terminal status to land on. `FunctionStatus` and `WorkerStatus` stopped at `deleting`.

Two live consequences: on screen, a function the tenant deleted on purpose was indistinguishable from one that broke; and since nothing transitions out of `failed`, it **held its tier slot forever** — the same permanent lockout #163 fixed for the other four modules, except that fix keys on a `deleted` status these two did not have.

## 🔑 The typecheck baseline was a symptom, and it is now zero

`tests/ignite/04` has failed typecheck for weeks with `Type '"deleted"' is not assignable to type 'FunctionStatus'`, sitting in the accepted baseline as noise. **It was a test reaching for the status that should have existed.** With the union fixed it passes on its own — nothing was papered over.

The other baseline error (`tests/ignite/03`, duplicate `vi`) turned out to be a genuine one-line duplicate import and was removed. **`corepack pnpm typecheck` from `apps/web` now exits 0** — I verified that independently on this branch. The repo has no accepted typecheck errors left, which means the next one that appears is real.

## The decisions worth reviewing

**A failed *stop* does not count as a failed teardown.** Proxmox deletes running containers, and an already-down container cannot be stopped — treating that as failure would reopen the defect from the side. Only a container that could not be **deleted** keeps the record on `failed`, and the Herald outcome follows the same decision, carrying `undeletedLxcIds`.

**Ignite stopped re-declaring `FunctionStatus`.** It had its own copy of the union next to the platform one, which is how it drifted a member behind; it now re-exports the platform type, as Blaze already did.

**Existing `failed` rows are deliberately not rewritten.** The migration cannot tell a genuinely failed provision from a completed teardown misfiled as one, and guessing either way is worse than leaving them.

**The badges show a muted "Deleted", not the red "Failed" they showed before.** Both badge maps are `Record<Status, …>`, so the new member was a compile error until handled — the type did the reminding.

## ⚠️ Includes a migration (`0036`)

`ALTER TYPE … ADD VALUE IF NOT EXISTS` on both enums. Append-only, no row touched, no default or constraint referencing the new label. The header explains why ADD VALUE is safe inside the runner's transaction on PG 12+. Not applied — `db:apply` stays your call.

## Found, not fixed

- **`tests/ignite/03` is genuinely flaky**, pre-existing: it registers `vi.mock("@/lib/server/ignite/provisioner")` **twice**, and the second silently overrides the first — whose comment explains it returns a never-settling promise precisely to stop background store writes from racing later tests. Verified by stashing: baseline failed 3 of 4 runs. Deleting the second block is the likely fix but changes runtime behaviour.
- `postgres-backend.test.ts` is baseline-red because pg-mem cannot parse migration `0029`. Related: pg-mem also cannot parse `ALTER TYPE … ADD VALUE`, so if that suite is ever repaired, `0036` will need a shim or an explicit skip.

323 tests pass across ignite, blaze and the quota helper; the 15 failures are exactly the known-red `05` files that need a live server.

title: fix(web): stop seeding form state from effects
body:
`react-hooks/set-state-in-effect`: **36 → 0**, across 35 files. Total ESLint errors 143 → 107, exactly −36 with none introduced. Rebased on current main; typecheck exits 0 and `pnpm build` compiles every route.

They shared one shape — a dialog seeding form state from props inside an effect — so this is one pattern applied 35 times, not 35 problems.

## Techniques

**Shell + keyed form inside `DialogContent` (22 dialogs).** Radix unmounts the subtree on close, so the form's `useState` initialisers re-run on the next open; that deletes the effect's reset branch outright, and a `key` covers what remains — re-seeding when the dialog is repointed at a different record while still open. The exit animation survives because `DialogContent` itself stays under Radix's control.

**Derive during render, store nothing (5).** Where the state was only ever a function of other state. `mesh/create-network`'s child-prefix clamp is the interesting one: the effect version allowed the select and the submit payload to disagree for one render.

**`useSyncExternalStore` (2)** — only where the state is genuinely external: `SplitView`'s `matchMedia`, and `onboarding-checklist`, which was keeping a copy of localStorage in React state and filling the copy from an effect.

**Event handler instead of effect (2).** `iam/member-dialog`'s two reset effects were **dead code**: both tabs render inside `DialogContent`, so `!open` could only be true during the closing animation — they blanked the form as it faded out.

## A user-facing bug fixed as a side effect

The old effects listed query data in their dependencies, and the query client refetches every 30 seconds. **So typing into an SDN zone or the VNet firewall options was silently discarded on a timer.** The keys are on data-arrival identity rather than object identity, so that stops. I treated it as a bug rather than behaviour worth preserving — say the word if you disagree.

## Judgement calls worth your eyes

- **`migrate-dialog` deliberately gets no key.** Its effect listed only `[open]` behind an `exhaustive-deps` disable — the author wanted defaults chosen once per open and never revised. Mount-time initialisers reproduce that; a key would not.
- **`atlas/clusters` consumes `?create=true` on dialog *close*, not open** — stripping it while the dialog was up would flip the key underneath and close it again. Visible difference: the URL keeps the param for the dialog's lifetime.
- **Soft-navigating to `?create=true` while already on beacon/tide/nexus/atlas now remounts the page content**, resetting the search box and any pending delete target. Previously only the dialog opened.
- **`onboarding-checklist` now syncs across tabs** via the `storage` event, and holds the new value in memory before writing so clicks still work if localStorage is unavailable.

## What is NOT verified, plainly

There are no component or dialog tests in this repo, and I cannot log into the panel to click through them. Lint, typecheck and a successful build prove these files compile and no longer break the rule; **they do not prove 22 dialogs still behave correctly for someone typing into them.** The reasoning per case is above and the diff is readable, but this is the change of the day that most wants human eyes on the actual screens — particularly the SDN dialogs and the IAM ones.

The one suite touching changed code (`components/mesh/network-select.filter.test.ts`) passes 8/8.

title: fix(provisioning): the publish check, everywhere else
body:
Extends #167 to the five remaining sites: Tide, Spark, Herald, Email, and Atlas's half-fix. Same shape — on a failed publish the resource goes `degraded`, the endpoint is **not stored**, and the Herald event drops to `partial` naming the port, the error and the intended address. Rebased on current main; typecheck exits 0.

- **Tide and Spark** — the IPv6 branches are untouched, since there is no NAT to fail there.
- **Herald** withholds both `endpoint` and `lokiEndpoint`. The push URL is the one that matters: a shipper aimed at a dead URL drops silently, and the symptom is an empty log search hours later.
- **Atlas** was the half-fix — it awaited and read the result, then `console.error`d and marked the cluster active with its endpoint anyway. DNS sync still derives from the *intended* endpoint, so the name is right when the forward is repaired.

## Email needed more than "degraded"

The loop publishes five to seven well-known ports, and **which one is missing decides what the operator does next**. So each missing port is named with its consequence — 25 means inbound mail cannot be delivered and senders will bounce; 993 means mail arrives but no IMAP client can read it; 443 means the Stalwart admin API is unreachable, so mailbox and domain provisioning will fail. `ports` records only what actually published, because it is the record of what the server answers on.

The event also says plainly that **no reconciler covers Courier's forwards** — its ports are fixed well-known numbers rather than `base+vmid`, and it is absent from `network/desired-state.ts`. Promising automatic repair would have been false.

### Two companion changes that were not optional

**`ensureMailServer` rebuilds `failed`/`degraded`/`deleting` servers from scratch.** Recording a partial publish as degraded walked straight into that: it would have stood a second container up beside a running Stalwart holding real mailboxes, and leaked the first one — over a missing iptables rule. Degraded is now returned as-is. This is the kind of thing that makes a "safe" status change dangerous, and it was only visible by reading the callers.

**Two `status === "active"` gates now accept degraded** (domain-provider resolution and domain deprovision). The admin API is reached at the container's own address over 443 with no DNAT involved, so refusing every mailbox operation because POP3 is unreachable from the internet would be pure loss.

## Proof the tests are guards

The suite went from 7 cases to 25. Stashing the five provisioners: **12 fail, 13 pass**. The 12 are exactly the new failure paths (Tide 2, Spark 2, Herald 2, Atlas 2, Courier 4); the 13 green are the pre-existing Flux/Nexus cases plus all 6 new controls — every happy path, and the Tide IPv6 case, which guards against the fix turning "no forward needed" into "forward missing".

Worth noting how one case was caught: the first draft of "does NOT rebuild a degraded mail server" **passed on the old code**, because old code never produced degraded so the branch was unreachable. Rewritten to seed a degraded server directly and assert `createLxcContainer` is never called, it fails on old code — the difference between 11 and 12.

## Found, not fixed

- **Courier has no reconciler coverage at all** — absent from `PRODUCT_DESCRIPTORS` and the collector's loaders, so nothing re-applies its mail forwards after a reboot or a lost lock. The generic descriptor does not fit it (fixed ports, no stored endpoint), so it needs its own design.
- **Tide and Ignite share port base 7000.** The reconciler's fallback for a row with no stored endpoint is `portBase + vmid`, so two products can derive the same external port for different containers. Pre-existing and already in the kickoff, but slightly more reachable now that a degraded Tide deliberately stores no endpoint.
- `ignite/provisioner.ts:84` is still fire-and-forget, owned by another change.

205 tests pass across the required suites; lint clean on touched files.

title: docs: the second wave, and the four findings under it
body:
Records #166–#171 and refreshes the header, which had drifted into contradicting the body.

## The line worth reading twice

This file listed two **"pre-existing accepted typecheck errors"** for weeks. One was a duplicate import. The other was a test reaching for the `deleted` status that did not exist — **the symptom of C7, sitting in plain sight in every typecheck run, filed as noise because the file said it was noise.**

`tsc --noEmit` now exits 0. There is no baseline, so the next error that appears is real. That is worth more than any single fix in these six PRs.

## Four findings registered, none fixed

**C10 🔴 — an Atlas credential you revoked keeps working.** `revokeAtlasCredential` never `DROP`s the role or sets `NOLOGIN`; revocation is a tombstone in the store. The row leaves the screen and the user keeps connecting and reading data. The product says access was withdrawn and it was not. Its neighbour: `regeneratePgHba` writes `deny` rules as `hostnossl`, which is not a deny — an SSL-less client still authenticates.

**C11 — Courier has no reconciler entry at all.** Absent from `PRODUCT_DESCRIPTORS` and the collector's loaders, so nothing re-applies its mail forwards after a reboot or a lost lock. The generic descriptor does not fit (fixed well-known ports, no stored endpoint), so it needs its own design.

**C12 — Atlas leaks replica containers.** `lxcIds` is only persisted at step 8, so a replica failing mid-loop leaves the store holding `[primaryVmid]` while already-created replica containers are orphaned; the failure path releases IPs and never deletes them.

Plus the smaller verified ones: `tests/ignite/03` is genuinely flaky (it registers the same `vi.mock` twice and the second silently overrides the first, whose comment explains why it must not be), `.audit-store.json` had no path override so the Atlas suite wrote test events into a developer's real audit file, and pg-mem cannot parse `ALTER TYPE … ADD VALUE` — relevant if the postgres-backend suite is ever repaired.

## A rule this session paid for

The runbook says `db:apply` runs **after** deploy. For an **additive** migration the new code depends on, that order breaks: without `0036` the enum rejects `deleted` and a teardown sticks in `deleting`. Additive goes before the deploy; destructive goes after, when nothing live depends on what it removes.

Both migrations are applied and verified independently — the Herald table held 0 rows before being dropped, and both enums were read back from `pg_enum`.

## One correction to my own record

I wrote in #161 that Tide awaited `addPortForward` correctly. It did not — `tide/provisioner.ts:263` fired it unawaited and published the endpoint on the next line. An agent checking the claim caught it; #171 fixes Tide along with Spark, Herald, Email and Atlas's half-fix.

Docs only.

title: fix(network): the reconciler covered Courier on paper and Nexus at the wrong port
body:
Two defects in the DNAT reconciler: one product it repaired into a black hole, one it did not cover at all.

## Nexus was declared on port 8081

`desired-state.ts` had `{ product: "nexus", internalPort: () => 8081 }`. The provisioner uses **9042** for ScyllaDB and **27017** for FerretDB. Nothing listens on 8081, so every "repair" the reconciler performed for Nexus installed a rule forwarding to nothing — and the cluster then read as reconciled.

The port now comes off the row's engine. The fallback is 27017 rather than a refusal, deliberately mirroring the provisioner's own `isScylla ? 9042 : 27017` — what is actually running in the container is the only thing that makes a DNAT rule correct, including its default branch.

## Courier: a descriptor entry would have been *inert*, not just wrong

This is the part worth reading. Courier does not fit the generic descriptor — fixed well-known ports instead of `base + vmid`, no stored endpoint, several forwards per server. But the failure of forcing it in is worse than ugly, and I verified it in the code before accepting the reasoning:

`collectForProduct` pushes to `unresolved` and `continue`s at lines 202–217 when `portBase` or `internalPort` yield nothing. **`extraForwards` is not consulted until line 260.** So a Courier entry in `PRODUCT_DESCRIPTORS` would sit in the list looking like coverage and emit exactly zero rules — the reconciler reporting that it covers something it does not, which is this codebase's signature defect wearing a config file.

So Courier gets its own collector alongside the generic one, and `COURIER_PORTS` is **derived from `email/config.MAIL_PORTS`** rather than copied — a hand-kept duplicate that drifts from what the provisioner opens is the exact failure this coverage exists to prevent. An unreadable email store lands in `failedProducts` and blocks `removeOrphans`, instead of reading as "there is no mail server".

## The removal safety argument

No removal code changed — `isManagedPort`, `MANAGED_PORT_RANGES`, `toRemove` and the `removeOrphans` default are untouched. The effect is one-directional: `toRemove` is drawn only from host rules with **no owner**, so adding desired forwards can only shrink the orphan set.

Concretely good: **port 4190 (Courier's ManageSieve) is the live production rule the earlier survey flagged as one `removeOrphans=true` away from deletion.** It now has an owner while a live mail server resolves, moving it from `toRemove` to `unchanged`.

`MANAGED_PORT_RANGES` was deliberately **not** widened: adds are not fenced by range, so widening buys nothing, while 25 and 443 would become deletable the moment the email store looked empty. And the forward's destination is resolved live from Proxmox for the recorded vmid, never from the stored address — which is what stops a stale row from having the reconciler point `443` at whoever inherited that IP.

Ownership is conditional (no live row, or an unresolvable container, and 4190 is an orphan again), so the reconciler header now says that plainly rather than claiming the hazard is closed.

## Found, not fixed

- **`MAIL_PORTS` has no 143** — plain IMAP is not forwarded, though Stalwart serves it. Possibly intentional (implicit-TLS only); **worth your confirmation**. If it is a gap, fixing `MAIL_PORTS` now fixes the reconciler automatically, which is the point of deriving rather than copying.
- **The CT-101 six (4317/4318/8123/5317/5318/8223) are still unprotected** — inside the managed range with no owner, so `removeOrphans=true` still takes them. Giving 4190 an owner is better than an allowlist entry for that one rule, but it is not a substitute for the port+destination allowlist the design doc still owes.
- **`isCompleteEnoughToDelete` only checks `failedProducts`** — a store that loads *empty* rather than throwing still authorises mass removal.
- **`email/store.ts` has only a singular `vmid`** while `memberNodes[]` anticipates multi-node; the collector reads only `vmid`, so a multi-node mail server would be under-covered. Not reachable today.

75 tests pass in `network/`, 221 across email/nexus/data-products; typecheck exits 0; zero lint findings in the touched files.

title: fix(ignite): the last unverified publish, and a test that was hiding a race
body:
The two Ignite leftovers, excluded from earlier PRs because another change owned the files.

## 1. The last unverified publish — and yes, this adds a status

`ignite/provisioner.ts` fired `addPortForward` without awaiting it, so a function went live advertising an endpoint that might forward nothing. It now awaits, reads the result, withholds **both** `endpointUrl` and `endpoint` when the publish failed, and emits `partial` to Herald with the port, the error and the intended address — the same shape as the other seven provisioners.

**`FunctionStatus` had no `degraded`, so this adds one**, which means a platform type change plus migration `0037` (ADD VALUE only, same shape as 0036). Stating it plainly because it is the bigger half of the change, and the alternatives lose for concrete reasons:

- `active` is the defect.
- `failed` is wrong twice: the provision did not die — the container is up and the runtime is serving on 8080 — and **nothing transitions out of `failed`**, so the function sits red forever holding the org's tier slot (quota releases only on `deleted`) while its LXC stays on the node. An operator reading "failed" rebuilds, and leaks the running container.
- `deploying` claims work in flight when nothing is running.

The decisive argument is the repair path: `network/desired-state.ts` already carries an `ignite` descriptor (base 7000 → 8080), `collect.ts` already feeds it, and its `LIVE_STATUSES` are `configuring | active | degraded`. **`degraded` is the only value that puts the function back where the reconciler can fix it** — and with no stored endpoint the reconciler falls back to `7000 + vmid`, which is precisely the rule that went missing.

Carried along: the badge is amber rather than red, the dashboard breakdown, the drizzle enum, and `DELETABLE_STATES` — which is an allowlist, so without adding `degraded` there a degraded function would have been the one thing a tenant could not delete.

## 2. The flake was hiding a real race

`tests/ignite/03` registered `vi.mock` for the provisioner **twice**; last-one-wins meant the second replaced the first, and the first existed specifically to return a never-settling promise so background store writes could not race later tests.

It is now one mock, and the three tests that trigger the fire-and-forget chain await a real happens-after signal (the function's `invocationCount` bump) rather than a sleep.

- **Before: 3 of 6 runs failed**, always the same assertion with a 404.
- **After: 11 of 11 passed.** I ran it twice more myself on the branch: 59/59 both times.

## Found and fixed in passing

`tests/ignite/08` stubbed `addPortForward` as resolving `undefined` — harmless while nobody read the result, and a thrown TypeError the moment the provisioner did, which would have sent every provision in that file to `failed`.

## Found, not fixed — one of them matters beyond Ignite

**The JSON store has no read-modify-write atomicity.** Every `saveX` does `load() → mutate → save()` over the whole file, so concurrent writers lose updates. That is what made this test race possible at all; the test-level drain hides it here, but **the same lost update is reachable in production JSON mode from any two concurrent requests.** Postgres mode is unaffected, and production runs Postgres — but the code default is `json`.

Also: `invokeFunctionService`'s success handler writes a stale snapshot (`{...fn, invocationCount: fn.invocationCount + 1}` from a read taken before the invocation began), so a concurrent update is silently reverted. The error handler already re-reads; the success path does not.

Typecheck exits 0 (rebuild `packages/platform` first, or the web typecheck fails on stale dist types). 273 tests pass across ignite and data-products; the 7 failures are the known-red `tests/ignite/05`, which needs a live server.

title: fix(atlas): revocation that revokes, denials that deny, replicas that clean up
body:
The 🔴 C10 plus its two neighbours.

## 1. A revoked credential kept working

`revokeAtlasCredential` never touched Postgres. It wrote a tombstone, the row left the screen, and **the role kept authenticating and reading data**. The product said access was withdrawn; it was not.

**`ALTER ROLE … NOLOGIN`, not `DROP ROLE`** — and the reasoning is the interesting part. Issuance grants the role `ALL PRIVILEGES ON DATABASE` plus `CREATE ON SCHEMA public`, so the first object it creates makes `DROP ROLE` fail with "objects depend on it". Reassigning ownership first is a decision about someone's data that a revoke endpoint has no business making. Combined with "a failed database operation must not report success", a drop that commonly fails is **a revocation that commonly leaves the access running**.

**Live sessions are terminated**, and the order matters: `pg_terminate_backend` runs *after* the NOLOGIN. Reversed, the pooler reconnects in milliseconds and it merely looks like it worked. These connections are pooled and live for days, so without this "revoked" would have meant "revoked whenever some unrelated process happens to restart". The two statements are separate execs so the half-failure — no new logins, old sessions surviving — gets its own message. Either failure returns `DEPENDENCY_UNAVAILABLE`: no tombstone, no audit event.

**A latent mismatch found on the way:** the store keeps the raw username while issuance writes `CREATE USER <sanitized>` **unquoted**, which Postgres folds to lower case. Both paths now share one `pgRoleName()`. Without it, revocation would have altered a role that does not exist and reported success against nothing — the same defect in a new place.

## 2. `deny` rules were not denials

`regeneratePgHba` wrote them as `hostnossl`, which is not a deny — an SSL-less client still authenticates. They are now `host … reject`, **in the operator's position order**. I deliberately did not hoist rejects above allows: "allow this host, reject the rest of its /8" and the inverse are both legitimate and differ only by order.

`assessCredentialAccess` now models exactly one provable lockout — a `/0` reject in the clients' own address family ordered above every applicable allow — and stays silent on narrower denies or missing positions. A screen that guesses a lockout sends people to delete rules that work.

## 3. Replica failures leaked containers

vmids are recorded on the cluster row the moment each container exists, and the failure path deletes what it created, releasing each Mesh address only once its container is confirmed gone. A survivor stays on `lxcIds` with its address still reserved and is named as `orphanedVmids` on the Herald event.

**One guard worth noticing:** a `finalized` flag stops the new destructive rollback firing after the cluster is recorded live. The trailing Herald emit is awaited, and previously a broken event bus only mis-set the status — with a rollback in place it would have destroyed a healthy database.

## Proof the tests are guards

Source stashed, tests kept: the revoke block gives **8 failures with 4 controls still passing**; firewall + replica-rollback + credential-access give **12 failures with 20 passing**. The controls that survive are the ones that should — the happy-path provision, `scram-sha-256` for allows, and every conservative "stays silent" verdict.

With the fix: 242 passing across atlas and the client-safe modules; typecheck exits 0. The one red file is `tests/atlas/05-e2e`, the known baseline that needs a live server.

## Found, not fixed

- `createAtlasCredential` still never inspects `result.exitCode`, relying on `execInContainer` throwing. Harmless today, but a second and weaker contract than the one revocation now uses.
- Re-revoking re-runs the SQL rather than short-circuiting on `revokedAt`. Deliberate — it repairs rows tombstoned by the old lying code — but a credential whose role was dropped by hand will report `DEPENDENCY_UNAVAILABLE` on a second revoke.
- `tests/atlas/03` mocked `execInContainer` as resolving a bare `""` rather than an `LxcExecResult`; corrected.
- `herald/events-store.test.ts` fails 3 pg-mem DDL tests on a clean tree too — unrelated.

title: docs(plano): portal do parceiro — vitrine de tenants com marca do cliente
body:
## O que é

Plano de execução para o **portal do parceiro**: um hotsite com a marca do cliente (primeiro: **consultoria**), onde o time dele cria e acompanha os tenants Catalisa dos clientes dele — clientes que **nunca vão acessar o painel**.

**v1 = vitrine + duas ações**: listar tenants, criar tenant, emitir token de API. Todo o resto continua no painel, como hoje.

Só documento. Nenhuma linha de código, nenhuma migration.

## O que foi medido antes de planejar

O plano parte do que existe, não do que se supõe:

| Achado | Consequência |
|---|---|
| `POST /auth/register` já cria IAM + org + usuário + billing | a criação de tenant **envolve** esse fluxo, não reescreve |
| `ref` já existe no contrato e é um `// TODO` logado | o vínculo parceiro→tenant é a peça que falta, não um mecanismo novo |
| **não existe modelo de parceiro** (`grep '^model (Partner\|Reseller\|Referral)'` = 0) | é o que há de genuinamente novo |
| sub-usuário **não é** tenant — o dado dele pertence ao master | os clientes do parceiro têm de ser masters-raiz; `parentId` faria o parceiro ver leads de todos juntos |
| token de API funciona ponta a ponta (`Bearer tok_` → guard global) | o mecanismo que a consultoria vai usar já está pronto |
| **sem assinatura o painel não abre** — o assistente toma a tela | criar tenant sem criar assinatura entrega cliente travado |
| `UserBranding` já tem a forma do whitelabel | reaproveitar a forma, não inventar outra |

## Conteúdo

- **5 decisões de arquitetura**, cada uma com o porquê de não ter reusado o que já existe
- **6 fases** com critério de pronto verificável (a da Fase 2: token emitido pelo portal responde 200 como aquele tenant — e não enxerga o tenant vizinho)
- **8 riscos** com mitigação, encabeçados por IDOR entre parceiros — mesma família dos 4 IDOR que a auditoria fechou este mês
- **5 questões abertas** para o dono; a principal: **o token precisa escrever, ou só ler?** Hoje `UserApiToken` não tem escopo, e "acompanhar" não deveria poder escrever

## Whitelabel

Default é **o nosso**: os 125 semantic tokens do painel, marca `#734B9C`. Whitelabel é sobreposição, então parceiro novo já nasce apresentável.

Os tokens são resolvidos **no `<head>`, antes do primeiro paint** — requisito, não refinamento: tema aplicado depois da montagem pisca roxo Catalisa antes de virar a cor do parceiro, e numa demo isso é o cliente vendo a marca do fornecedor.

## Pendência de insumo

`consultoria.com.br` responde **403 a fetch automatizado** — logo, cores e tipografia da consultoria não foram capturadas. Está registrado como primeiro item da Fase 0.

title: chore(backup): the survey, and the scheduler that was not dead
body:
The owner asked whether the backup and snapshot features reuse each other or duplicate and overlap, and wants lean code. This is the survey (`docs/backup-surface-survey.md`), plus two safe cleanups.

## ⚠️ First: I was wrong, and the way I was wrong is the point

I briefed this work saying `data-products/backup-scheduler.ts` was **dead code** — "nothing imports it except its own test". **That was false.** Its caller is `apps/web/instrumentation.ts:12`, which lives *outside* `src/`, is what Next.js runs at server boot, and reaches it through a dynamic `import()` inside an `if`.

My grep was scoped to `src/`. The caller is not in `src/`.

Had the agent trusted me and deleted it: no test would fail, no route would 500, `tsc` would stay green — and **scheduled Spark backups would simply stop**, with `lastBackupAt` quietly ageing on every cluster until somebody needed a restore. That is the same failure this codebase keeps producing, in its most expensive form. "Dead code" proven by a grep over the wrong directory is not proven.

So it was **moved**, not deleted: to `spark/backup-scheduler.ts`, where it always belonged — it imports `SparkCluster` and hardcodes `engine === "memcached"` — with a header recording what nearly happened. Verified by grepping every `.ts/.tsx/.js/.mjs/.json` outside node_modules for all four exported names.

## The map

Five surfaces, ranked by how real they are.

**Spark is the only one that takes data, moves it, and can put it back** — BGSAVE, poll `INFO persistence`, `mc cp` the RDB to a dedicated Tide; restore is the same path backwards, verified with `DBSIZE`. About 550 lines, already well factored. **Forge/vzdump** and **Forge/snapshots** are thin wrappers over Proxmox, and the snapshot dialog is *already* correctly shared between the VM and CT pages. **Atlas has no backups and honestly returns 501.** Tide, Flux, Nexus, Blaze, Herald and Ignite have nothing at all.

**The overlap that looks biggest is superficial.** A vzdump, a Valkey BGSAVE and a qemu snapshot share a noun and nothing else — "snapshot" means a vzdump *mode* in one dialog and the *thing created* in another. Unifying them would require lying about two of the three. That is the answer to "are we duplicating": mostly no, and the one place we are is small.

## What changed

The vzdump option lists were hand-written in both `backup-job-dialog` and `run-backup-dialog` and **had already drifted** — compression read "ZSTD (recommended)" in one and plain "ZSTD" in the other. Extracted to one module.

Nothing else was touched: not the Atlas 501, not its retained scaffolding table, nothing crossing package boundaries.

## Ranked next, with the first one being a real user-facing bug

1. **The vzdump storage picker offers storages that do not exist.** `local` / `nfs-backup` / `pbs-backup` are the **mock server's** three storages. On this hardware two are invalid and the third is the small root-backed pool that `storage-defaults.ts` exists to avoid. `restore-backup-dialog` already does it right by reading the node's storages. First on the list because it is the only item that fails on the user's first click.
2. **Atlas's `walEnabled` badge** — stored, defaults true, rendered as a green "WAL on", and nothing sets `archive_mode`. The last survivor of the fake-backup episode.
3. **`BackupApi` implemented twice**, in `core` and in `forge`, same five methods and endpoints; `sdk` wires forge's and nothing constructs core's. The hazard is concrete: forge inlines its paths, so a route change made in core's `API_PATHS` never reaches the copy that actually runs.
4. **`fmtDate` in five byte-identical copies.** Ranked last precisely because it is the easiest and the least reviewable.

**Not recommended:** a unified backup abstraction. If Atlas ever gets real backups they will be `pg_basebackup` plus WAL shipping — a third mechanism. What would be worth sharing then is the due-time arithmetic and the retention count, not the act of backing up.
